Glossary

Every term a newcomer meets in Chapters 1 to 10, in the order the chapters bring them up. On the other pages, a word with a dotted underline opens its entry.

Gaussian (peak-one bell)
A smooth weight that falls off exponentially with the squared distance from a center, measured in units of the widths. In this manual it peaks at 1.
Weight field, positive widths
A weight field is a number at every point in space: 1 at the center, falling off with distance. The three widths are a splat's sizes along its own axes; they must be above zero.
Mean, center μ
The position where the bell has its largest weight.
Standard deviation, axis width s
A length that measures distance along one of a splat's own axes. It is a yardstick, not a hard radius: the ideal weight is still about 0.14 at two widths.
Covariance Σ
A symmetric 3-by-3 matrix that holds the squared widths and the way the axes are turned, Σ = R S ST RT. Terms off the diagonal mean the axes are tilted.
Quadratic form
An expression in which every term has two factors of the input. In two dimensions, ad1² + 2bd1d2 + cd2². With 4 and 1 on the diagonal it is 4d1² + d2², and setting it to 1 draws an ellipse. The exponent of a Gaussian holds one [5].
Tilt, rotation
Tilt is the off-diagonal terms of Σ: zero when a splat's axes line up with x, y, and z. Rotation is a splat's own turn. "Tilt lock" is a different thing: the camera control in Chapter 5.
Anisotropic, isotropic
Different widths along the axes, or equal widths in every direction. A plain kit splat is isotropic; the flat discs that cover a surface are anisotropic.
Quaternion q
Four numbers that describe a rotation. They only describe a rotation when their length is 1, so a reader scales them to length 1 first.
Affine
A straight-line map plus a shift, p ↦ Ap + b. Straight lines stay straight [6].
Footprint
The patch of the screen where one splat can add any color.
Jacobian J
The matrix of the projection's slopes at one point, used as a straight-line stand-in for the projection near the splat's center.
Opacity α, transmittance T
Opacity says how much a splat covers. Transmittance is how much of what lies behind still shows after the splats in front: the product of (1 − a) over them.
Alpha compositing
Laying colors over one another in order, each weighted by its opacity and by how much of the pixel is still uncovered.
Spherical harmonics
A compact way to store how a color changes with the direction you look from. Many trained captures store them; a kit splat has one base color.
Recipe, capture
A recipe is a program that makes splats. A capture is a file of splats fitted to photographs of a real thing.
Kit, kit toy
The kit is Splashery's toy-building library. A recipe names shapes, colors, and moving parts, and the kit fills them with splats in the browser, spreading the budget evenly by area. A kit toy is built this way; a scan or capture is loaded from a file.
Smoothstep
The curve 3g² − 2g³, an S-shaped ramp from 0 to 1 that is flat at both ends, used to start and stop a motion gently [7].
Grammar, atom
A grammar is a list of rules for what counts as a valid program. In it, = is "is made of", | is "or", { } repeats, [ ] is optional, and quotes mark text typed exactly. An atom is the smallest piece of an expression that can stand alone [8].
u, v, t, morph
u and v are the coordinates of the flat sheet of points that each splat gets a place on, before the equations bend it into shape. They are parameters of a parametric surface, not a substitution [9]. t is time: 0 to 2π in the equation language, and the toy's running time in a recipe's drive. A morph is a splat sliding from its own place to a target place.
Kernel
The rule for how a splat's weight falls off across its patch. The site normally draws a cut-off Gaussian; a labs setting can use a sharper one. Neither is the ideal bell.
Part, token
A part is a group of a toy's splats that moves as one solid piece, such as a lid or a sail. Every splat carries the number of its part; number 0 is the body, so a toy has up to 15 more (Chapter 2). A token is one of up to 48 separate pieces, such as a game piece, that a recipe moves by its own offset.
Drive
The function in a recipe that runs every frame and says how the toy looks now: the angle of each part, the glow, the page of a sheet. It does not move splats itself; it hands numbers to the graphics chip.
Splat budget, tier
The number of splats the toy is asked to draw. It depends on the device: a tier (low, mid, high, or max) sets a default count and a ceiling, and a recipe may ask for more or fewer per base budget with its density. The counts run from 60,000 up to 400,000.
Pack
A file under src/packs/ that holds the recipes of a group of toys.
Labs switch
The setting that shows the toys and tools not yet ready for everyone. Add ?labs=1 to the site's address to turn it on (the browser remembers it) and ?labs=0 to turn it off. A link to a labs toy opens it either way; the switch only decides what the shelf shows.
Seed
A number that starts a repeatable stream of pseudo-random numbers. The same seed gives the same toy every time, which is why a link can rebuild it.
Sorting, back to front
Splats are partly see-through, so they must be drawn from the farthest to the nearest for the blending to come out right. The engine sorts them for the camera; a toy that moves its splats may need them sorted again where they stand.
Uniform, shader
A shader is a small program that runs on the graphics chip for every splat. A uniform is a value the page hands it once a frame, the same for every splat, such as a part's rotation. Hands-on play, a recipe's drive, and the controls all reach the screen as uniforms.
Level of detail
Drawing less where little shows: a big structure gets fewer splats per atom, and a page far away gets a coarser sheet.
Web worker
A background thread of a page. Heavy jobs (reading a file, turning a page into splats, training) run in one so the page stays smooth.
Sheet, leaf, spine
A sheet is a flat place in a toy where a picture shows (Chapter 5). A leaf is a sheet that turns like a page, about a spine.
Hands-on, rigid body
Hands-on is the ✋ switch: a drag picks up the toy and a let-go tosses it. A rigid body is a thing that never changes shape, described by its place and its turn; most toys play as one (Chapter 6).
Position-based dynamics (XPBD)
A way to simulate physics by moving things to where they would be if nothing overlapped and every joint held, then working out their speeds from how far they moved. Splashery's own engine uses an extended form of it [11, 12].
Joint: hinge, slider, dial, socket, break
The ways a part may move in hands-on play. A hinge swings about an axis, a slider moves along a line, a dial turns round and round, a socket lets a loose piece click back into its place, and a break lets a piece snap off when pulled hard. Each of the first three is moved by one number, an angle or a distance.
Node, skin
A node is one point of a rope or a cloth, held to its neighbors by links. A splat that follows two nodes (or four, for cloth) is called a skin splat: the rope bends and the splat stays whole.
Restitution (bounce)
The share of its speed a thing keeps after a bounce: a basketball dropped on a hard floor keeps about 0.82 to 0.88.
Toy radius
The unit of length hands-on play uses: the toy's own radius. Gravity, throws, and the play area are given in toy radii, so every toy falls the same way whatever its size on screen.
Ångström, B-factor
An ångström is a tenth of a nanometer; atoms in a bond are about 1 to 2 of them apart. A B-factor says how much an atom's place is blurred in a crystal, by motion or disorder.
Voxel
A volume pixel: one little cube of a 3D scan, with one number for how dense the material is there.
Window and level, Hounsfield unit
A window picks the range of values that show, from a lower to an upper level, and the rest is hidden or faded. In a CT scan the values are in Hounsfield units, on which water is 0 and air is about −1000.
Point cloud, lidar, LAS and LAZ
A point cloud is a list of points with places and sometimes colors. Lidar makes one by timing laser pulses. LAS is the standard file for them; LAZ is the same file compressed.
Magnitude
A scale on which each step is a fixed ratio. An earthquake's magnitude goes up by one for about 32 times the energy. A star's magnitude goes the other way: the smaller (or more negative) the number, the brighter the star, and 6 is about the faintest the unaided eye sees under a dark sky.
Precession, sidereal time, J2000
Precession is the slow wobble of the Earth's axis, one turn in about 26,000 years, which shifts where the stars are. Sidereal time is time measured by the stars instead of the Sun, and tells which part of the sky is overhead. J2000 is the moment (January 1, 2000, noon) a star catalog's positions are given for.
Snapshot, feed
A feed is a web address that serves current data, such as the earthquakes of the past week. A snapshot is a dated copy of that data that ships with the site, for when the feed cannot be reached.
Depth map, relative depth
A picture the same size as a photo whose every pixel holds how far away that part is. A depth model's map is relative: it says which parts are nearer than which, not how many meters. Often it is stored as disparity, which is large for near things.
Sharp view, relief
A second view of the photo toys that lays the photo, at its full resolution, on a relief: a surface lifted by the same depth the splats use. It is a textured surface, not splats.
Training, gradient descent
Gradient descent nudges numbers again and again in the direction that lowers an error. Training a splat scene is gradient descent on the splats' places, sizes, colors, and opacities until pictures drawn from them match the photos [1].
Structure from motion
Working out where the camera was for each of many overlapping photos, and where the points they show lie in space.
WebGPU, WebAssembly
WebGPU is the browser's newer way to use the graphics chip for general computation, which Video to 3D needs for training. WebAssembly is a compact code format that runs at near native speed; the depth model runs on it through ONNX Runtime Web.
PLY, SOG, SPZ, .splat
Splat file formats. PLY is the plain one that every tool reads and that keeps everything. SPZ is about a tenth of its size and keeps view-dependent color. SOG is the smallest and keeps base colors only. .splat is simple and keeps base colors only.
Module, finder pattern, quiet zone
A module is one cell of a QR code. The three big squares in the corners are the finder patterns, which let a reader find and orient the code. The quiet zone is the blank border, four modules wide.
Error correction, Reed–Solomon, codeword
A QR code holds extra codewords (8 modules each) made with a Reed–Solomon code [19], so a reader can rebuild the text if some are lost. The level (L, M, Q, or H) sets how many: about 7, 15, 25, or 30 percent of the codewords.
QR version
The size of a QR code, from 1 (21 modules on a side) to 40 (177). A longer text needs a higher version.
Halftone, error diffusion
Showing a picture with only dark and light dots. Error diffusion decides each dot by passing the error of the last choice on to the pixels beside it.
Check digit
A digit of a barcode worked out from the others, so a reader can tell when it has misread one.
Fragment, deflate, base64url
The fragment of a link is everything after the #; a browser never sends it to a server. Deflate is the compression of zip files and PNG pictures; a Splashery link uses its raw form. Base64url spells bytes with the 64 letters, digits, -, and _ that are safe in an address.
Scene
Everything needed to rebuild a view: the toy, its options, the look, the camera, and any paint, written as JSON. A link is a scene; a scene file is the same scene saved as a file.
